demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: It begins three years ago on a Tuesday in late October. The phone rings at 3:14 a.m. She answers it, hears the frantic voice of a dispatcher, then static, then the wet crack of tires losing traction on a highway. She drops the receiver onto the kitchen tiles. That sound echoes in her head every time a car door slams, every time a motorcycle backfires, every time her own device vibrates against a wooden table. She is sixty now, and the years have not softened the fracture. She wakes before dawn, as she has since that night. The dark feels familiar, but it carries weight. Her husband, Arthit, sleeps beside her, breathing steadily. She lies on her back, eyes open, tracing the shadows on the ceiling. She thinks of him—Daeng—how he used to call every Sunday with stories of his rambutan trees, how his laughter used to fill their mother’s house. Now the house is quiet. When he died, the world split into a before and an after. She tries to stitch it back together by following routines, but the threads slip through her fingers. At work, she sits in the fourth row of the customer service floor. Her headset rests lightly on her ear, the microphone positioned near her mouth. She has handled over twenty thousand calls in her twelve years with the company. Today, her supervisor has set a new performance metric: average handle time. The queue fills with urgent requests. A woman’s voice crackles through the earpiece, speaking quickly about a billing error. The pitch of the voice, the urgency, the way the words pile up—they pull at a hidden wire in her chest. Her breath shortens. She focuses on the script on her monitor, reading each line aloud, but the letters blur. She repeats her opening greeting three times, then catches herself, clears her throat, and starts over. During breaks, she steps into the stairwell, pressing her palms flat against the cool concrete wall until her heartbeat slows. She tells herself it is just work. But her body knows the difference between a customer’s frustration and a crisis that cannot be resolved with a solution. At home, she prepares dinner with meticulous care, slicing vegetables into uniform strips. Arthit asks about her day. She answers in fragments, then stops. She worries that if she speaks too loudly, she will break the fragile calm she has built. They watch the news together in the evenings, but when the weather segment mentions heavy rain and road accidents, she changes the channel. She drives to the market only on weekends, choosing side streets, scanning the mirrors long before a car approaches. When a delivery motorbike cuts too close, her hand flies to her chest. She does not yell. She simply closes her eyes and counts to ten, the same way she learned to do in the hospital waiting room. She sits in her therapist’s office now, hands folded in her lap. The afternoon light falls across the wooden floor, illuminating dust motes that drift like slow memories. She speaks of the quiet mornings, the phantom ring of her phone, the way she flinches when a colleague’s chair scrapes against the tiles. She talks about missing him with a precision that surprises her. The grief has not softened; it has simply changed shape, settling into the creases of her days. She finishes her sentence, pauses, and looks out the window. A sparrow lands on the sill, tilts its head, and flies away. She watches it go, breathes evenly, and waits for the next unspooling hour.
